faults.fault: the explanation skipping the causal step
faults.finding: 'the peak of its slosh, V I sin φ, measures how much' states the size without showing where it comes from.
faults.fix: Tie it to lesson 4: the quarter-cycle part times the voltage is lesson 4's slosh, whose peak was 70.7 V × 7.07 A = 500 W, so with only I sin φ of the current the peak is V × I sin φ.

faults.fault: the explanation skipping the causal step
faults.finding: 'the current must double ... because only its in-step part does the work' leaves the reader to work out why it doubles.
faults.fix: Say the in-step part, I cos φ, must stay at 7.07 A to keep 500 W, so at cos 60° = 0.5 the whole current is 7.07 ÷ 0.5 = 14.1 A.

faults.finding: 'none of these steps depends on the frequency' fails for Q = I²X, where X does.
faults.fix: Say none of the steps from meter readings depends on the frequency.

faults.finding: 'The current ... follows S, not P' holds only at a given voltage.
The Q readout's sign for a leading current is never said, yet screen 11 speaks of '250 var leading'; screen 12 writes S = P = 50 W, giving apparent power in watts.
faults.fix: Say the Q readout shows a minus sign when the current leads (−250 var on screen 11), and write S = 50 VA and P = 50 W.

faults.fault: misconception from the brief not caught
faults.finding: The brief's 'parts in place of sizes' slip (power worked from the in-step part of the current) has no DO screen; screen 8's 1150 W option repeats screen 4's volts-times-amps slip.
faults.fix: Replace the 1150 W option with 756 W, the in-step part of the current squared, (5 × 0.87)² × 40.

faults.finding: Screen 4 asks for a true power by V I cos φ, but screen 3 never states the rule or names true power.
faults.fix: End screen 3 by stating P = V I cos φ and naming it the true power.

faults.finding: 1652 var and 1600 W appear in practice but are not listed.

shape.idea named up front: yes, paragraph 1: the power wave dips below zero, watts used, vars sloshing back, volt-amps supplied, and the cable carries the current of the long side
shape.rule in words: yes: P = V I cos φ from the in-step part, Q = V I sin φ from the quarter-cycle part, S = V × I, P² + Q² = S², power factor P ÷ S = cos φ
shape.worked example with real numbers: yes: the slosh at 60° (250 W, 433 var, 500 VA), lesson 6's bench (24 W, 32 var, 40 VA), the motor in practice
shape.misconception shown failing: yes: V × I taken as watts (screens 2, 4), plain subtraction (screen 6), V² ÷ R with the whole supply and the in-step current (screen 8), the gap taken as heat (screen 10), sin for cos and 'leading returns nothing' (screen 11), vars added (screen 12)
shape.analogy with where it breaks: yes: a tug's towline at an angle; breaks because the sideways pull moves no energy while vars really travel out and back
shape.put it into practice: yes: safety first, steps, rule of thumb, worked example (the course's motor puzzle), mistakes

verdict: rewrite as draft 2 with the eight fixes
